subject: CRS
category: The Synoptic Gospels and the Synoptic Problem
question: Discuss at least five contents of the gospel according to Matthew
modelAnswer:
Matthew's Gospel (28 chapters) contains (any five):
1. The genealogy and birth of Jesus (ch. 1–2): the genealogy from Abraham through David; the angel's message to Joseph; the birth in Bethlehem; the visit of the wise men (Magi); the flight into Egypt and Herod's killing of the children; the return to Nazareth.
2. The ministry of John the Baptist, Jesus' baptism and temptation (ch. 3–4).
3. The Sermon on the Mount (ch. 5–7): the Beatitudes, salt and light, Jesus' teaching on the law, anger, adultery, divorce, oaths, retaliation, love of enemies, almsgiving, prayer (the Lord's Prayer), fasting, treasures in heaven, anxiety, judging others, the golden rule and the two foundations.
4. Miracles (ch. 8–9): healing of a leper, the centurion's servant, Peter's mother-in-law, calming the storm, the Gadarene demoniacs, the paralytic, Jairus' daughter and the woman with a haemorrhage, the blind and the dumb.
5. The mission of the Twelve (ch. 10).
6. Parables of the kingdom (ch. 13): the sower, the weeds, the mustard seed, the leaven, the hidden treasure, the pearl and the net.
7. Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi and the founding of the church (16:13–20); predictions of the passion; the transfiguration (ch. 17).
8. Teaching on church life and forgiveness (ch. 18).
9. The triumphal entry, cleansing of the temple and controversies in Jerusalem; woes against the scribes and Pharisees (ch. 21–23).
10. The end of the age and judgment (ch. 24–25): the ten virgins, the talents, the sheep and the goats.
11. The passion narrative (ch. 26–27): the Last Supper, Gethsemane, arrest, trials, Peter's denial, Judas' death, crucifixion and burial.
12. The resurrection and the Great Commission (ch. 28): 'Go therefore and make disciples of all nations ... and lo, I am with you always.'
Throughout, Matthew stresses the fulfilment of Old Testament prophecy.

subject: CRS
category: The Synoptic Gospels and the Synoptic Problem
question: Examine the characteristics of the gospel of Mark as a Christian
modelAnswer:
Note: 'as a Christian' is taken as part of the question's wording; the answer explains the characteristics and what they mean to a Christian.

Characteristics of Mark's Gospel:
1. Shortest of the Gospels (16 chapters) and probably the earliest (about AD 65–70); used as a source by Matthew and Luke.
2. A Gospel of action: it records more of what Jesus did than what He said; the word 'immediately' (euthys) occurs over forty times, giving a fast-moving narrative.
3. Vivid, eyewitness detail, traditionally from Peter (e.g. 'the cushion' in the boat, 4:38; 'green grass', 6:39; Jesus' emotions such as anger, pity and sighing).
4. Jesus as the Son of God (1:1; the centurion's confession, 15:39) and as the suffering Son of Man and Servant who came 'not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many' (10:45).
5. The 'Messianic secret': Jesus often commands silence about His identity and miracles (1:44; 3:12; 8:30).
6. Emphasis on the cross: about a third of the Gospel deals with the last week of Jesus' life; three predictions of the passion (8:31; 9:31; 10:33–34).
7. Written for Gentile (probably Roman) readers: Jewish customs are explained and Aramaic words are translated; Latin words are used.
8. Honest portrayal of the disciples' weaknesses and lack of understanding.
9. Few long discourses and parables compared with Matthew and Luke; no birth narrative; it begins with John the Baptist.
10. The original ending is uncertain: the best manuscripts end at 16:8.

Meaning to a Christian: discipleship means following Jesus on the way of the cross, serving others, and trusting the Son of God who has power over sickness, nature, demons and death.

subject: CRS
category: The Synoptic Gospels and the Synoptic Problem
question: Who is the gospel of Luke addressed to?
modelAnswer:
1. The person addressed: Luke addressed his Gospel to 'most excellent Theophilus' (1:3), probably a Roman official or a person of high rank (the title 'most excellent' was used of governors, Acts 23:26), possibly a new convert or an enquirer. The name means 'lover of God', so some think it stands for any Christian reader.
2. The purpose for him: 'that you may know the truth concerning the things of which you have been informed' (1:4), i.e. to give an orderly, reliable account to confirm his faith.
3. The wider audience: Gentile Christians and the Greek-speaking world in general. Evidence: Luke traces Jesus' genealogy back to Adam, the father of all humanity (3:38); he explains Jewish places and customs; he uses Greek rather than Aramaic terms; he dates events by Roman emperors and governors; and he stresses that salvation is for all people, including Gentiles, Samaritans, women, the poor and sinners.
4. The same Theophilus is addressed in Acts (1:1), so the two books were written as a pair for the same readers.

subject: CRS
category: The Synoptic Gospels and the Synoptic Problem
question: Define Synoptic problem and proffer solution
modelAnswer:
Definition: the Synoptic Gospels are Matthew, Mark and Luke, so called because they can be 'seen together' (Greek synopsis) side by side. The Synoptic Problem is the question of how to explain the literary relationship among them: they share a great deal of material, often in the same order and with nearly identical wording, yet they also have important differences.
Evidence: about 90% of Mark is found in Matthew and over 50% in Luke; Matthew and Luke share about 230 verses not found in Mark (mostly sayings of Jesus); each Gospel also has material of its own (M for Matthew, L for Luke).

Proposed solutions:
1. Oral tradition theory: the similarities come from a common, fixed oral tradition of the apostles' preaching, not from copying documents. Weakness: it does not explain the exact verbal agreements in Greek.
2. Two-Source (two-document) hypothesis, the most widely accepted: Mark was written first (Markan priority); Matthew and Luke each used Mark and another common source of sayings called Q (from German Quelle, 'source'). Reasons for Markan priority: Matthew and Luke rarely agree against Mark in order; Mark's rougher style is often smoothed out by Matthew and Luke.
3. Four-Source hypothesis (B.H. Streeter): Mark, Q, M (Matthew's special material) and L (Luke's special material).
4. Augustinian hypothesis: the Gospels were written in canonical order, Matthew first, Mark used Matthew, and Luke used both.
5. Griesbach (Two-Gospel) hypothesis: Matthew was first, Luke used Matthew, and Mark combined and shortened both.
6. Farrer hypothesis: Mark first, Matthew used Mark, and Luke used both Mark and Matthew, without the need for Q.

No solution answers every difficulty, but the Two-Source/Four-Source approach is the one most scholars accept.

subject: CRS
category: Literature and Theology of the Synoptic Gospels
question: Why is Jesus' birth so important to the world?
modelAnswer:
1. Fulfilment of prophecy: Jesus' birth fulfilled Old Testament promises, e.g. a virgin conceiving a son called Emmanuel (Isaiah 7:14; Matthew 1:22–23) and a ruler born in Bethlehem (Micah 5:2; Matthew 2:5–6).
2. The incarnation: God became man ('Emmanuel', God with us); the eternal Son took human flesh, so God is known personally.
3. Salvation: the angel said, 'You shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins' (Matthew 1:21); 'to you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, who is Christ the Lord' (Luke 2:11).
4. Good news of great joy for all people (Luke 2:10): the birth was announced to poor shepherds, and wise men from the East came to worship, showing the Saviour is for all nations, rich and poor, Jew and Gentile.
5. Peace and goodwill: 'Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among men with whom he is pleased' (Luke 2:14).
6. Demonstration of God's love and humility: the Son of God was born in a manger, identifying with the poor and humble.
7. Light to the Gentiles and glory to Israel (Simeon, Luke 2:32).
8. Hope and a new beginning for humanity: the beginning of the new covenant and of God's kingdom among people.
9. It is celebrated worldwide at Christmas, uniting Christians and promoting love, giving and reconciliation.

subject: CRS
category: Literature and Theology of the Synoptic Gospels
question: Why is Jesus' teaching on the Fatherhood of God so important to Christians
modelAnswer:
Jesus taught that God is 'Father', using the intimate word 'Abba' (Mark 14:36), and taught His disciples to pray 'Our Father who art in heaven' (Matthew 6:9–13; Luke 11:2–4).

Importance to Christians:
1. It reveals God's nature as personal, loving and caring, not distant or harsh.
2. It gives believers a close, personal relationship with God as His children, and the right to approach Him freely in prayer.
3. Providence: the Father feeds the birds and clothes the lilies, and knows what His children need, so they should not be anxious (Matthew 6:25–34).
4. He answers prayer and gives good gifts, including the Holy Spirit, to those who ask (Matthew 7:7–11; Luke 11:13).
5. Forgiveness: the parable of the prodigal son (Luke 15:11–32) shows a Father who welcomes repentant sinners; Christians must also forgive as they are forgiven.
6. Brotherhood of believers: if God is the Father of all, Christians are brothers and sisters and should love one another and even their enemies, 'so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven' (Matthew 5:44–45).
7. A standard for living: 'You, therefore, must be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect' (Matthew 5:48); good works should glorify the Father (5:16).
8. Assurance and security: the Father's will is that none of His little ones should perish (Matthew 18:14); He rewards those who seek Him in secret (6:4, 6, 18).

subject: CRS
category: Literature and Theology of the Synoptic Gospels
question: Define resurrection and state the different appearances of Jesus after resurrection as written in the synoptic gospel
modelAnswer:
Definition: the resurrection is the rising of Jesus Christ from the dead, bodily and alive, on the third day after His crucifixion and burial, by the power of God. It is the foundation of the Christian faith (1 Corinthians 15:14).

Appearances in the Synoptic Gospels:
1. To the women at the tomb (Matthew 28:9–10): Mary Magdalene and the other Mary met Jesus, who said 'Hail!'; they took hold of His feet and worshipped Him, and He told them to tell His brethren to go to Galilee.
2. To Mary Magdalene first (Mark 16:9–11, in the longer ending of Mark).
3. To two disciples on the road to Emmaus (Luke 24:13–35; Mark 16:12–13): Cleopas and his companion recognised Him in the breaking of bread.
4. To Simon Peter (Luke 24:34).
5. To the Eleven and others in Jerusalem (Luke 24:36–49; Mark 16:14): He showed His hands and feet, ate broiled fish, opened their minds to the Scriptures and promised the power from on high.
6. To the Eleven on a mountain in Galilee (Matthew 28:16–20): some worshipped, some doubted; He gave the Great Commission: 'All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore and make disciples of all nations ... I am with you always.'
7. At the ascension near Bethany (Luke 24:50–51; Mark 16:19).

Note: Mark's oldest manuscripts end at 16:8 with the empty tomb and the angel's message; the appearances in Mark 16:9–20 are in the longer ending.

subject: CRS
category: Literature and Theology of the Synoptic Gospels
question: Narrate the ascension account of Jesus as written in the synoptic gospel.
modelAnswer:
The ascension is recorded in Luke 24:50–53 and in the longer ending of Mark (16:19–20); Matthew ends with the Great Commission in Galilee without describing the ascension (Acts 1:6–11, also by Luke, gives a fuller account).

Luke's account: after appearing to the disciples in Jerusalem and teaching them, Jesus led them out as far as Bethany. He lifted up His hands and blessed them. While He blessed them, He parted from them and was carried up into heaven. They worshipped Him and returned to Jerusalem with great joy, and were continually in the temple blessing God.
Mark's account: after the Lord Jesus had spoken to them, He was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God. The disciples went out and preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the message by the signs that attended it.
(Acts 1:9–11 adds that a cloud took Him out of their sight and two men in white robes said that He would come back in the same way.)

Significance: it marks the end of Jesus' earthly appearances; His exaltation to God's right hand; the beginning of the disciples' mission; and the promise of His return.
